question: What is the main purpose of the Compound Components pattern?

options.text: Speed up component rendering through memoization
options.explanation: Compound Components is an architectural pattern for API design, not a performance optimization

options.text: Avoid using TypeScript in components
options.explanation: Compound Components work great with TypeScript and are even better typed than the render props approach

options.text: Reduce the number of files in the project
options.explanation: Compound Components don't reduce the number of files — on the contrary, each sub-component can be a separate function

options.text: Provide a declarative flexible API instead of passing everything through props
options.explanation: Compound Components allow the component user to control the structure declaratively, avoiding prop explosion

question: Why is it recommended to use Context instead of React.Children + cloneElement?

options.text: Context is faster on large trees
options.explanation: Context can cause unnecessary re-renders — this is not an argument in its favor from a performance standpoint

options.text: TypeScript types Context better than cloned elements
options.explanation: cloneElement with additional props loses types; Context is strictly typed via createContext<T>

options.text: Context is an explicit contract, cloneElement is implicit magic
options.explanation: With Context, the component's dependency on the parent is explicit via a hook; cloneElement implicitly adds props without the receiver's knowledge

options.text: A special license is required for this
options.explanation: The listed technologies have open-source versions.

options.text: cloneElement works only for direct children, Context works for any nesting level
options.explanation: Context passes through any depth of the tree, cloneElement passes props only one level down

question: What happens if you call useTabsContext() outside of a <Tabs> component?

options.text: Context returns the last saved value
options.explanation: Context is not cached globally — outside the Provider it always returns the initial value (null in our case)

options.text: Nothing — React simply ignores the call
options.explanation: React doesn't ignore hook calls — if the hook has a throw, it will throw an error

options.text: It returns undefined
options.explanation: createContext(null) returns null as the initial value, not undefined

options.text: An error with a clear message will be thrown, if the hook is implemented correctly
options.explanation: Correct implementation: if ctx === null, throw new Error('...must be used within <Tabs>'). This is better than a cryptic TypeError

question: You are creating a <Select> component with Compound Components. How does Select.Option know its index in the list for keyboard navigation?

options.text: Option counts its previous sibling elements via the DOM
options.explanation: Accessing the DOM to determine logical order is a poor approach — it's fragile and violates the React model

options.text: The index is not needed — Option always knows whether it's selected by the selected value
options.explanation: To display the focused state when navigating with arrows, focusedIndex is needed — knowing just selected is not enough

options.text: The user must pass index explicitly: <Select.Option index={0} value='ru'>
options.explanation: This is possible but inconvenient — the user has to manually count indices. A good API does this automatically

options.text: Option automatically receives the index via React.Children.map in the root component
options.explanation: SelectRoot traverses children via React.Children.map, collects all values from Option components, and stores them in an options array in context. Option looks up its index in this array

question: Why use Object.assign(TabsRoot, { Tab, Panel, List }) instead of just exporting TabsRoot?

options.text: It allows writing <Tabs.Tab> instead of <TabsTab>, creating a namespaced API
options.explanation: Object.assign creates a single object with nested components — this is a convenient namespaced API, clear and auto-completable

options.text: This is the only way to create Compound Components in React
options.explanation: You can also assign static properties: TabsRoot.Tab = Tab. Object.assign is just one convenient way

options.text: Object.assign speeds up component rendering
options.explanation: Object.assign just creates an object with the needed properties — it has no effect on rendering performance

options.text: TypeScript automatically infers sub-component types from the Object.assign result
options.explanation: The return type of Object.assign includes the types of all added properties — autocomplete and type checking work out of the box

question: In which case is the Compound Components pattern NOT a good choice?

options.text: When the component structure is fixed and the user shouldn't change it
options.explanation: If the structure is always the same (e.g., a simple card with avatar + name + bio), a prop-based API is simpler and clearer

options.text: When the component is used in several places in the application
options.explanation: Reusability is a good reason for Compound Components — they provide flexibility without rewriting the component

options.text: When the component has several interconnected parts
options.explanation: Several interconnected parts is the main signal for using Compound Components

options.text: When the component is part of a design system
options.explanation: Design systems are an excellent place for Compound Components: they give users flexibility while maintaining consistency

question: How should you properly organize keyboard navigation in Select.Options?

options.text: Add an onKeyDown handler to the root element of the component
options.explanation: onKeyDown on the root div with tabIndex={0} is the correct approach: the event bubbles up from the Trigger button and is handled centrally

options.text: All of the above options are incorrect
options.explanation: Some of the listed options are indeed correct.

options.text: Handle keydown on window via addEventListener
options.explanation: Global handlers are bad practice: they fire even when Select is not focused and can conflict with other components

options.text: Close the list when Escape is pressed
options.explanation: Escape to close is standard expected behavior (ARIA Authoring Practices Guide), without it the component is inconvenient for users

options.text: Call e.preventDefault() when ArrowDown and ArrowUp are pressed
options.explanation: Without preventDefault(), the arrows will scroll the page in parallel with option navigation — this is undesirable behavior

question: You are creating a <Stepper> and want each <Stepper.Step> to know its ordinal number without explicitly passing stepIndex. How to implement this?

options.text: Use useId() to generate a unique id for each Step
options.explanation: useId() generates unique strings but doesn't determine order — this doesn't solve the numbering task

options.text: Each Step independently counts the number of previous Steps via querySelectorAll
options.explanation: DOM queries to determine logical order are an antipattern: fragile, only works after mounting, violates the React model

options.text: Use React.Children.map in StepperRoot and pass stepIndex via cloneElement
options.explanation: React.Children.map traverses children, cloneElement adds stepIndex to each Step. This is the classic way to automatically number child components

options.text: Store totalSteps in a ref and increment on each Step mount
options.explanation: Incrementing on mount is unreliable: mount order is not guaranteed, and with dynamic step addition the counter will break

question: Why add displayName to Compound Components sub-components?

options.text: For correct TypeScript operation
options.explanation: displayName is a runtime property only for debugging; TypeScript uses static types and doesn't depend on displayName

options.text: For server-side rendering (SSR) to work
options.explanation: SSR works without displayName — this is exclusively a developer tool for debugging

options.text: For readable names in React DevTools
options.explanation: Without displayName, anonymous functions appear as Anonymous or Component in DevTools. With displayName 'Tabs.Tab' the tree becomes readable

options.text: For re-render optimization via React.memo
options.explanation: React.memo uses component referential equality, not displayName — these are unrelated

question: How does controlled mode differ from uncontrolled mode in Compound Components?

options.text: In controlled mode, state is stored outside the component and passed via props
options.explanation: Controlled: <Tabs activeTab={active} onTabChange={setActive}> — the parent controls the state

options.text: A good component supports both modes simultaneously
options.explanation: The pattern: if activeTab is passed — use it (controlled), otherwise use internal useState(defaultTab) (uncontrolled)

options.text: Controlled mode is always faster due to fewer re-renders
options.explanation: Controlled mode can cause more re-renders since the parent component also re-renders on state change

options.text: In uncontrolled mode, state is stored inside the component via useState
options.explanation: Uncontrolled: <Tabs defaultTab='home'> — the component manages state on its own, external code receives changes via callback
